default.What it looks like: Among the most stable places in the sample. Politics rarely disrupts daily life or business. Institutions generally work, disputes go through courts and elections, and the economy has buffers. Risk comes mainly from unexpected shocks.

Broadly functional, with specific weak spots. Most things work most of the time, but there are soft spots: a stretched budget, patchy governance or pockets of unrest. Disruptions happen, and are usually contained and short.

Material risk on more than one front. Expect periodic protests, policy surprises or economic stress. Contracts and plans can be upset by events outside your control, so they need contingencies and regular review.

Serious, persistent risk. Instability, weak institutions and/or economic crisis are part of normal operating conditions. Working there takes active risk management: security planning, financial safeguards and local advice.

Among the most dangerous and fragile places in the world. War, the near-collapse of the state or a deep economic crisis. Daily life and business are heavily disrupted; outside presence is often limited to essential humanitarian, diplomatic or security work.

flags.Threshold: War-level violence (≥1,000 battle deaths in a year, UCDP threshold)
flags.In real life: Armed conflict is killing people on a scale that counts as war or active conflict. Fighting can move fast, cut roads and supply lines, and spill into neighbouring areas.
flags.Common response: Most governments advise against travel to affected areas; organisations limit presence to essential staff with security plans, and insurers treat the area as a war zone.

flags.Threshold: Active armed conflict (≥25 battle deaths in a year, UCDP threshold)
flags.In real life: Armed conflict is killing people on a scale that counts as war or active conflict. Fighting can move fast, cut roads and supply lines, and spill into neighbouring areas.
flags.Common response: Most governments advise against travel to affected areas; organisations limit presence to essential staff with security plans, and insurers treat the area as a war zone.

flags.In real life: Prices are rising fast, so wages, savings and fixed-price contracts lose value month by month. Fast price rises often set off cost-of-living protests and strikes.
flags.Common response: Businesses index contracts to inflation or price them in hard currency, review salaries and cash transfers often, and buy stock before prices rise.

flags.In real life: Prices are rising fast, so wages, savings and fixed-price contracts lose value month by month. Fast price rises often set off cost-of-living protests and strikes.
flags.Common response: Businesses index contracts to inflation or price them in hard currency, review salaries and cash transfers often, and buy stock before prices rise.

flags.In real life: The economy is shrinking: weaker demand, layoffs and falling tax revenue, which can sour the political mood and squeeze the government's budget.
flags.Common response: Firms cut sales forecasts, review the credit risk of local customers and prepare for layoffs and wage disputes.

flags.In real life: Public debt is high, leaving little room to respond to a shock. Tax rises, spending cuts or an IMF programme become more likely, and in the worst case a debt restructuring.
flags.Common response: Investors check their exposure to government bonds and public-sector clients, and treat budget announcements and IMF talks as risk events.

flags.In real life: The government spends far more than it collects. That usually ends in tax rises, spending cuts, money printing or late payments to suppliers.
flags.Common response: Suppliers tighten payment terms with government clients and plan for tax changes.

flags.In real life: The country relies on foreign money to pay for its imports, which leaves the currency vulnerable if investors pull back.
flags.Common response: Firms hedge or reduce their currency exposure and review supply chains that depend on imports.

flags.Threshold: Thin FX reserves (<3 months of imports)
flags.In real life: The central bank has little foreign currency left: less than three months of imports. Import restrictions, dollar shortages, capital controls or a devaluation often follow.
flags.Common response: Firms keep extra stock of imported inputs, convert local earnings to hard currency promptly, and check the rules on moving money out of the country.

flags.In real life: A quarter or more of young people who want work can't find it. Youth unemployment is a well-documented driver of protest movements and emigration.
flags.Common response: Employers invest in local hiring and training; analysts watch campuses, social media and fuel or food price decisions as protest triggers.

flags.In real life: At least one person in twenty has been forced from their home. Needs for shelter, food and health care are large, and neighbouring countries carry heavy pressure.
flags.Common response: Humanitarian agencies scale up through UN-led coordination; donors and host governments plan for long-term displacement as well as emergency relief.

flags.In real life: Violent crime is high, at twenty or more murders per 100,000 people a year, and it affects residents, staff and visitors.
flags.Common response: Organisations adopt crime-specific security measures: vetted transport, secure accommodation, restrictions on night travel.
